reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Pain is referred to the head from a disorder of the cervical spine, typically the upper C1 to C3 segments
It is usually side-locked and unilateral without side-shift, beginning in the neck or occiput and radiating to the fronto-temporal region
Attacks are provoked by neck movement, sustained awkward postures, or pressure over the upper cervical joints or muscles
Restricted cervical range of motion and ipsilateral neck, shoulder or arm discomfort are common
Relief of pain after a diagnostic anaesthetic block of a cervical structure or nerve strongly supports the diagnosis
Autonomic and migrainous features are usually mild, helping distinguish it from migraine and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias
Imaging changes of cervical spondylosis are common with age and do not by themselves confirm causation
reference.pathophysiology: Cervicogenic headache arises because sensory afferents from the upper three cervical segments converge with trigeminal afferents in the trigeminocervical complex of the upper spinal cord and lower brainstem. Nociceptive input from the upper cervical joints, discs, ligaments or muscles is therefore perceived as pain in trigeminal territory, that is, in the head, and the pattern of referral depends on the specific cervical structure generating the pain.
additionalDifferentials: Migraine, especially when accompanied by neck pain
additionalInvestigations: Examination of cervical range of motion and provocation of pain by neck manoeuvres
Assessment of upper cervical joint and muscle tenderness
Cervical spine imaging with X-ray or MRI when structural or red-flag features are present
Diagnostic anaesthetic blocks of cervical facet joints or nerves for confirmation
Review for migrainous features to distinguish overlapping headache types
redFlags: Neurological signs of cervical myelopathy or radiculopathy
A history of significant neck trauma, malignancy or infection
Systemic symptoms, fever or unexplained weight loss
Sudden severe neck pain with headache suggesting arterial dissection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cervical disorder; many patients improve with physiotherapy, manual therapy and targeted injections, though pain can be chronic and recurrent when degenerative changes persist.
pitfalls: Attributing headache to incidental cervical spondylosis seen on imaging
Missing vertebral or carotid artery dissection presenting with neck pain and headache
Confusing it with migraine, which also frequently involves neck pain
Relying on imaging rather than on clinical provocation and diagnostic blocks
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cervical source with physiotherapy comprising manual therapy, cervical mobilisation, targeted neck strengthening and postural correction
Provide symptomatic analgesia while limiting reliance on simple analgesics to avoid medication-overuse headache
Offer a diagnostic and therapeutic anaesthetic block of the implicated cervical facet joint or a greater occipital nerve block, both to confirm the source and relieve pain
Consider radiofrequency neurotomy of the responsible cervical medial branches when blocks give reproducible but temporary relief
Advise ergonomic and postural modification and avoidance of sustained awkward neck positions that provoke attacks
Refer to a headache specialist or pain service for chronic or refractory pain and to reassess for coexisting migraine
